# Event-Driven Architecture, Worked Out

> An interactive, single-page explainer for event-driven architecture: what a broker actually
> guarantees (Kafka, SQS, SNS, EventBridge), why Server-Sent Events is a transport rather than an
> architecture, and how AI model streaming and multi-agent orchestration both ride on the same
> mechanism. The SSE parser
> and DAG scheduler shown are verified against real running code by `test-model.ts`; broker guarantees
> are cited from official docs. Author: Paweł Pasek.

Key points made on this page:

- **Foundations** — a producer doesn't know its consumers; an event is a fact, not a request, so a
  failed consumer doesn't un-happen it; coupling moves from runtime calls to schema shape.
- **Delivery guarantees** — Kafka is at-least-once by default (exactly-once needs an idempotent
  producer plus a transactional, read-committed consumer); SQS standard is at-least-once/best-effort
  order, SQS FIFO is exactly-once/ordered within one Message Group ID; SNS/EventBridge fan out with no
  cross-subscriber ordering (SNS FIFO topics excepted).
- **Ordering and parallelism** — order is scoped to a Kafka partition or an SQS Message Group ID,
  never to a whole topic/queue. A partition is also the unit of consumer parallelism, so ordering and
  throughput are bought with the same currency: picking a key is picking how small a scope stays
  ordered. Consumers within one group compete for each event; separate groups each get their own copy.
- **Event shape and schema evolution** — three shapes in Fowler's terms (event notification,
  event-carried state transfer, event sourcing). Coupling lands on the payload: adding an optional
  field is the only broadly safe change, a rename breaks every reader at once, a type change breaks
  them silently, and a genuinely breaking change means publishing a new event type beside the old one
  — fact 1 means the producer cannot enumerate who to warn. Whether an addition is safe is a fact
  about the consumer's content model (`additionalProperties: true` vs `false`), not about the event.
- **SSE is a transport, not an architecture** — it *breaks* fact 1: the server holds one identified
  client's connection and writes straight down it. The event-driven half is the in-process bus
  (emit/subscribe/bounded replay buffer); SSE is the wire that carries its output across a process
  boundary to a browser, and `subscribe(event => res.write(...))` is the adapter between them. One
  HTTP response kept open, `Content-Type: text/event-stream`, wire fields
  `data:`/`event:`/`id:`/`retry:`, one direction only; `EventSource` auto-reconnects using
  `Last-Event-ID`.
- **AI streaming** — the same SSE mechanism with a documented schema:
  `message_start` → per-block `content_block_start/delta/stop` → `message_delta` → `message_stop`.
  Tool-call input arrives as JSON fragments (`input_json_delta`/`partial_json`) safe to parse only
  once the block closes.
- **Agents** — a multi-agent system is a DAG of tasks reacting to `done` events; the ready set
  (dependencies all satisfied) is recomputed every round, mirroring an event loop's phases one level up.
  Nobody draws the DAG: agents build it at runtime by calling `delegate_task`, whose
  `dependsOnTaskIds` argument becomes the edge — the same tool call that arrived as `partial_json`
  fragments over SSE. That tool call is a *command* (imperative, refusable, awaited); what the
  scheduler emits afterwards (`task.completed`) is an *event* (past tense, addressed to nobody).
- **Event sourcing** — state is recovered by folding an append-only event log, not stored directly;
  crash recovery and an audit trail come for free, until the log needs compaction.
- **Failure handling** — a redelivered event under at-least-once delivery isn't a bug; the real
  backoff formula this page verifies is `min(15000, 1500 * 2^(attempt-1))` ms (jitter-free as quoted,
  which invites a thundering herd); a message failing past a retry limit belongs in a dead-letter
  queue.
- **Idempotency** — `balance += amount` double-counts a redelivery; `balance = balanceAfter` doesn't,
  which makes it an event-shape decision rather than a consumer fix; a dedup table works but must be
  written in the same transaction as the effect, or it is the dual write again, and its retention
  window is the real limit of deduplication (SQS FIFO: 5 minutes). Idempotent is not order-proof — an
  absolute write applied out of order is idempotent and still wrong without a version guard.
- **The dual write** — you cannot write to a database and publish an event atomically. The outbox
  pattern makes it one local transaction plus a relay; change-data-capture derives events from the
  database's own replication log instead, at the cost of your table schema becoming the public
  contract. Sagas and end-to-end exactly-once are named and left out.
- **What you give up** — no stack trace (a correlation id only if you added one beforehand), no "find
  all callers", eventual consistency as a visible UX problem, testing that moves to the seams between
  services, and a broker to operate. With one service, one database and one consumer you deploy
  together, write the function call: if you can name your consumer, you don't yet have what events
  buy.

## Page

- [Event-Driven Architecture, Worked Out](https://pasekpasek.github.io/event-driven-architecture-worked-out/): the full explainer.

## Source material

- [Apache Kafka documentation — message delivery semantics](https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/#semantics)
- [Apache Kafka — Introduction](https://kafka.apache.org/intro): partitioning, per-partition order, and partitioning as the scalability mechanism.
- [Martin Fowler — "What do you mean by Event-Driven?"](https://martinfowler.com/articles/201701-event-driven.html): event notification, event-carried state transfer, event sourcing, CQRS.
- [Confluent Platform — Schema Evolution and Compatibility](https://docs.confluent.io/platform/current/schema-registry/fundamentals/schema-evolution.html): BACKWARD/FORWARD definitions and the JSON Schema content-model caveat.
- [AWS SQS developer guide — message deduplication ID](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/using-messagededuplicationid-property.html): the 5-minute deduplication window.
- [AWS SQS developer guide — FIFO queues](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-fifo-queues.html)
- [AWS SQS developer guide — dead-letter queues](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html)
- [AWS SNS developer guide — FIFO topics](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/sns-fifo-topics.html)
- [AWS EventBridge user guide — dead-letter queues for undelivered events](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eventbridge/latest/userguide/eb-rule-dlq.html)
- [Anthropic Messages API — streaming](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/streaming): the "Streaming request with tool use" response quoted verbatim as this page's §07 fixture.
- [4th-devs](https://github.com/i-am-alice/4th-devs), `05_01_agent_graph/src/{events.ts,server.ts,scheduler/*,tools/task/delegate.ts}` and `03_02_events/docs/{heartbeat.md,schemas.md}`: the real event bus, SSE server, DAG scheduler, the `delegate_task` tool that builds the graph, the backoff formula and the heartbeat loop this page is built from.
- WHATWG HTML — the `text/event-stream` parsing algorithm `EventSource` implements.

## Caveat

Five of the page's models are checked by `test-model.ts` (21 checks): the SSE parser against a real
HTTP server, the DAG scheduler against an independently-written oracle port (including the blocked
child case), the backoff formula against its source, the §05 schema-evolution matrix verdict by
verdict, and the §10 idempotency models. Broker delivery/ordering guarantees (Kafka, SQS, SNS,
EventBridge), Confluent's compatibility definitions and Fowler's taxonomy are cited from primary
sources, not independently reproduced locally. The §07
streaming fixture is quoted from Anthropic's own published documentation, not captured from a live
API call.
